readingInstruction: Read Romans 12:1-13:14. Paul turns from doctrine to its practical results. Notice the word “therefore” that begins chapter 12, the call to a living sacrifice, the community ethics, and the instructions on government and love.
settingTheScene: The first eleven chapters of Romans explain what God has done. Chapter 12 begins, “I appeal to you therefore, brothers, by the mercies of God.” The mercies of God, everything described in chapters 1 to 11, are the basis for all Christian living. Doctrine leads to doxology (11:33-36) and then to duty. What follows is a practical guide for the believer’s life in the church, in the world, and under the government.
observation: “I appeal to you therefore, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God, which is your spiritual worship” (12:1).
“Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind” (12:2).
“So we, though many, are one body in Christ, and individually members one of another” (12:5).
“Let love be genuine. Abhor what is evil; hold fast to what is good” (12:9).
“Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good” (12:21).
“Let every person be subject to the governing authorities. For there is no authority except from God, and those that exist have been instituted by God” (13:1).
“Owe no one anything, except to love each other, for the one who loves another has fulfilled the law” (13:8).
“But put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh, to gratify its desires” (13:14).
interpretation:
“By the mercies of God.” The appeal is not based on threats or fear, but on mercy. Because God has saved us, we offer ourselves. “Present your bodies as a living sacrifice.” In the Old Testament, sacrifices were killed. Now we are living sacrifices, daily offering everything to God: hands, feet, time, money, vocation. This is “your spiritual worship” (or “reasonable service”). Worship is not only singing on Sunday; it is the whole of life offered to God.

“Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind.” The world presses us into its mold, and the Spirit transforms us from within. As the mind is renewed by the word of God, we are able to discern God’s will, “what is good and acceptable and perfect.”

Paul next calls for humility and sober judgment. We are one body with many members, and each has gifts: prophecy, serving, teaching, exhorting, giving, leading, mercy. Each is to be used with the right attitude: generosity, zeal, cheerfulness. Then follows a series of short commands on love in action, verses 9 to 21: genuine love, brotherly affection, outdoing one another in showing honor, not slothful in zeal, fervent in spirit, serving the Lord, rejoicing in hope, patient in tribulation, constant in prayer, contributing to saints’ needs, practicing hospitality. “Bless those who persecute you; bless and do not curse them. Rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep. Live in harmony with one another.” “Never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God.” And the climax: “If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him something to drink… Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.”

Chapter 13 opens with a subject that has caused much discussion: governing authorities. “Let every person be subject to the governing authorities. For there is no authority except from God.” Government is a gift of God for restraining evil and promoting good. Christians should pay taxes and give respect where it is due. Paul was writing under Nero. Most interpreters note that this does not mean unlimited obedience: Peter and John said, “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29). When governments command what God forbids, believers must obey God. But the default is respect and cooperation.

Then Paul returns to love. “Owe no one anything, except to love each other, for the one who loves another has fulfilled the law.” Love sums up the commandments. He closes with urgency: “The night is far gone; the day is at hand.” The return of Christ is nearer than when we first believed. So “cast off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light.” The last command is perhaps the best summary of sanctification: “Put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh, to gratify its desires.” This was the verse that Augustine read in the garden, and which led to his conversion.
connection: Leviticus 1 and Hebrews 13:15-16 speak of sacrifice. Ephesians 4:1-16 and 1 Corinthians 12 speak of the body and gifts. Proverbs 25:21-22 is quoted in verse 20. Deuteronomy 32:35 is cited in verse 19. 1 Peter 2:13-17 and Titus 3:1-2 speak of government. Mark 12:17 says to render to Caesar. Acts 5:29 and Daniel 3 and 6 show the limits of obedience. Revelation 13 is another view of the state. Matthew 22:37-40 and Galatians 5:14 say love fulfills the law. Ephesians 6:10-18 speaks of armor.
application:
Offer your body as a living sacrifice today. Choose one specific thing: your schedule, a talent, a habit.

Renew your mind by reading Scripture first, before the news.

Look for an enemy or difficult person to bless, and do something kind.
prayerPrompts: Present your body to God as a living sacrifice, and say what that means today.
Ask him to renew your mind.
Ask him to help you love without pretense.
